articles.title: Inside a global AI company built in rapidly-growing India
articles.text:
A global AI health company built in rapidly-growing India
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Oct 16, 2026
Inside a global AI company built in rapidly-growing India
Qure.ai uses AI for early detection of diseases. Its CEO thinks India will be on the forefront of AI use.
The Age of Workby Kai Ryssdal, Nela Richardson, Andie Corban and Sarah Leeson
Download
Before founding Qure.ai in 2016, CEO Prashant Warier got his masters and PhD in the United States.
Sarah Leeson/Marketplace
In our series “ The Age of Work,” Marketplace is looking at how changing demographics are reshaping the global economy.
Last month, “Marketplace” host Kai Ryssdal and ADP Chief Economist Nela Richardson, our project partner on the series, travelled to Mumbai, India, for the latest installment. India — with a median age of 29 — is a few years away from its demographic peak.
Qure.ai
Qure.ai is based in Mumbai, India, but it’s growing worldwide — including in the United States, where it has 26 clearances from the Food and Drug Administration. The company uses AI for early diagnosis of lung cancer and tuberculosis, among other health tech tools.
“The advantage that we had here was that we had access to a lot of data,” said Prashant Warier, co-founder and CEO of the company. “The number of people that go into any hospital in India is probably multitudes larger than any other system in other parts of the world, and so we had access to a lot of data to train the algorithms.”
Another advantage to being in India, Warier said, is the talent of its workforce. Ryssdal and Richardson visited Qure.ai’s headquarters and spoke to several of its young tech workers.
“It’s the kind of talent that would go study at Stanford and then work at Google or Microsoft,” Warier said.
Ryssdal and Richardson talked to him about the current narrative around artificial intelligence in the United States — namely, some people being afraid of the technology and what it could mean for their jobs.
“The fact is that everywhere outside of healthcare, AI is taking away people’s jobs because it is doing things that people can do,” Warier said. “But I think in healthcare, it can do things that people can’t do, and it can actually improve outcomes. So, I think healthcare is one of those places where it is creating a better world and increasing the GDP of the world.”
Warier noted India has had a tech-savvy population, “from the days of Y2K,” he said, and that he thinks the country will also be on the forefront of AI use.
The view of India’s economy from a major business district
Ryssdal and Richardson wrapped up their time in Mumbai in a business district called BKC, or the Bandra Kurla Complex, which is full of bank buildings, a WeWork skyscraper, and the first Apple Store in India.
“There is only one way an economy grows, and that’s if there are more workers, and those workers become more productive,” Richardson said. “I have faith that the economy always wins.”

articles.title: What are the economics of putting on a marathon or 5K race?
articles.text:
How much does it cost to host a marathon or 5K?
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Oct 16, 2026
What are the economics of putting on a marathon or 5K race?
It's getting tougher for organizers to host races thanks to inflation, tariffs and greater competition for cash sponsorships.
I've Always Wondered ...by Janet Nguyen
Race organizers constantly have to deal with unexpected challenges, whether that's sinkholes or tariffs.
JasonDoiy/Getty Images
This is just one of the stories from our “I’ve Always Wondered” series, where we tackle all of your questions about the world of business, no matter how big or small. Ever wondered if recycling is worth it? Or how store brands stack up against name brands? Check out more from the series here.
Samantha Janes asks:
I'm a big 5K and half marathon runner. There are a ton in Florida, so I drive to different events around the state to participate. I've always wondered what it takes to hold a successful 5K or half marathon sporting event and what the economics behind it look like.
Planning for a successful 5K or half marathon is often a year-long process that requires managing dozens of staff members, liaising with city officials, navigating financial challenges and dealing with unforeseen obstacles.
"I've had issues with sinkholes in the middle of our route. The day before, the road collapsed and we had to completely change our course" said Michael Clemons, director of operations at Running USA, a nonprofit organization that advocates for the running industry.
Racing events like 5Ks (more than 3 miles) and half marathons (more than 13 miles) are making just enough to break even, a goal that's challenging due to the high expenses associated with putting on a race, tariffs, and greater competition for cash sponsorships, experts told Marketplace.
Putting on a 5K in a smaller market can cost anywhere from $10,000 to $15,000, while a 5K in a large city can cost between $500,000 to $1 million, Clemons said. Meanwhile, half marathons can cost between $50,000 to $75,000 in a smaller market to upwards of $1 million in larger ones.
As the numbers above demonstrate, those costs can change depending on which part of the U.S. you're in and where you're hosting your race.
The Sacramento Running Association puts on local 5K races at parks that can cost under $10,000, said Scott Abbott, the executive director of SRA.
"The running industry isn't a huge financial boon"
Many organizations that put on these races are nonprofit organizations that use them to help fundraise money.
"You see the Alzheimer's Association putting on a walk or a run, or you see pride organizations putting on runs that support the LGBTQ+ community and the efforts that are there to support queer individuals, either in the running space or beyond," Clemons said
There are also for-profit organizations that put on 5Ks or races, although they often still fundraise for a cause.
"The half marathons tend to be for-profit organizations more than 5Ks, just because of the amount of work that goes into it," Clemons said. "A lot of the charitable organizations don't have a dedicated staff or the resources to put on longer races by themselves, so they may look to a for-profit organization to put on the race."
But even if a for-profit organizes a race, there might still be a fundraising component to it. The organization might donate a percent of the proceeds from the raise to a charity, or the individuals who are racing might fundraise for a charity of their choice, Clemons said.
"The running industry isn't a huge financial boon. A lot of what we do is going back to support our communities, going back to support charities. So it's either a break-even or just enough money to cover the costs of what we need to do to support our communities," Clemons said.
Race expenses
Road closures are one of the biggest costs for organizers. You have to pay police officers — who are often working overtime rates — to shut down these roads and provide traffic support, Clemons said.
"It is expensive to close down three miles of roadway, especially if you're in a major city, like if you're in Atlanta or in Los Angeles," Clemons said.
The cost of shutting down roadways in Louisville, Kentucky — which is a big market, but not a major one — can set you back $75,000, Clemons said.
A small 5K event where there are only one or two closures might leave you with a police bill of $3,000 to $4,000, Abbott said.
You also have to pay for medals, T-shirts, and post-race items like water, bananas and other food, which have gone up in price due to tariffs, Clemons said. T-shirts might cost $7 to $10 a person, while medals could cost $3 to $5 a person, Clemons said.
While races rely on volunteers, they also pay some staff members, like the people who time the race. Some might pay for a timing company, which could have a base cost of $1,500, along with a cost-per-participant fee on top of that, Abbott said.
Each runner has a bib and a timing chip to track their progress, and that might be $1 to $1.50 per runner, Abbott said.
"There are multiple timing companies that all have different rates, and a lot of times they might work with a nonprofit, if it's a small event to try to make it within their budget," Abbott said. "But sometimes if the event's very small, it may not be worth it in its first year to have it be a timed event because of that cost."
A 5K could have as few as one or two staff members, and a volunteer group of 10 to 20, while a major half marathon can have a staff of 50 and a volunteer group of 1,000, Clemons said.
"We rely on volunteers to help support a course as course marshals, to help hand out medals at the finish line, to help with the check-in process. So there are ways that you can get creative with volunteers, but it's also really important to not cut the corners too much, where you're sacrificing the safety of participants or you're sacrificing the overall event experience," Clemons said.

articles.title: Who are the people who set earnings expectations?
articles.text:
Who are the people who set earnings expectations?
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Oct 9, 2026
Who are the people who set earnings expectations?
Analysts at the major banks set these expectations, with guidance from the companies themselves, experts told Marketplace.
I've Always Wondered ...by Janet Nguyen
Companies try to manage earnings expectations so that they don't end up underperforming when they release their reports.
M. Santiago/Getty Images
This is just one of the stories from our “I’ve Always Wondered” series, where we tackle all of your questions about the world of business, no matter how big or small. Ever wondered if recycling is worth it? Or how store brands stack up against name brands? Check out more from the series here.
Allen Tang asks:
You often hear that a company beat or missed "expected" earnings. My question is who are the people or entities that make these expectations, why do their opinions have so much power to move stock prices based on their "expectations," and where does the public get access to this information?
News about a company's earnings for the quarter will always mention whether it beat analysts' predictions.
Sell-side analysts at brokerages and investment banks who follow these companies are the ones setting these expectations, said Eric So, a professor of global economics and behavior science at MIT. That can include the likes of Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs.
"Data providers like FactSet, Bloomberg, and LSEG average those forecasts into a consensus estimate. That consensus is the benchmark people mean when they say a company beat or missed," So explained.
Management at the company itself will also set their own expectations, said Patrick Badolato, a professor of instruction in accounting at the University of Texas at Austin. When they do, they'll often give a range of what you might expect in the coming quarter instead of a specific figure, Badolato said.
"Analysts can change or update their expectations based on what management does," Badolato said. "Analysts can also change with respect to what other analysts do."
Analysts will set these targets based on a host of factors depending on the type of company and industry, including historical performance, consumer trends and the foot traffic at a company's stores.
You can find consensus estimates for free on Yahoo Finance and Nasdaq, while the company's own guidance is available to the public in earnings releases and calls, So said.
Companies are going to try to manage expectations so they can avoid underperforming relative to the targets that they release publicly.
"Analyst forecasts tend to start out optimistic and then get walked down as the announcement approaches, frequently after guidance or conversations with the company, so the bar ends up just low enough to clear. As a result, far more companies narrowly beat consensus than narrowly miss it," So said. "Analysts have reasons to go along, since playing along with managers’ preferences to create beatable targets tends to buy them access to management, which is valuable to their clients and their careers."
Even though the companies themselves help manage expectations, sometimes they can still get things wrong.
That's because when you make projections, there might still be weeks worth of business to be conducted, Badolato said. Macroeconomic events can also alter metrics in your earnings report, while contracts can be pushed off, and input and labor costs can change, Badolato added.
"We're always dealing with change and uncertainty in the world. So I would say we should expect them to be imperfect," Badolato said.
You can't get away with lowering your targets too much just so you can say you beat expectations, because then people will catch on, said Matthew Spiegel, a finance professor at Yale University.
"The analysts will go, 'Well, you know, gee, they just said this, so it must be 10% higher,'" Spiegel said.
Beating expectations can change the stock price for the simple reason that it's now more valuable than what experts predicted.
"If I thought the firm was going to earn $100 for me this quarter, and it actually earned $110, I'd be pretty happy. And if someone wanted to buy the stock from me, I'd probably charge them a little more, right? The firm is doing better than I thought it was, so it's worth more than I thought," Spiegel said.
Conversely, if the firm does poorly relative to what you thought, you'd have to offer the stock at a lower price if you want to get rid of it, Spiegel said.
"The person buying it is gonna go, "Well, you might have thought it was gonna earn 100 bucks, but they're only earning 90, so we're not gonna give you as much," Spiegel said.
Failing to meet expectations can also signal that there are other aspects about the company — like its long-term revenue trajectory — that the market didn't know about, Badolato said.
Basically, the market is admitting that it had incomplete information, Badolato said.
A small discrepancy between a company's earnings and expectations usually won't shift the company's stock price that much though, Spiegel said.
"When you see a small discrepancy in the earnings announcement and a huge change in the stock price, there's something else going on at the same time," Spiegel said.
A company may have announced that another firm plans to buy them, or maybe there were issues at one of their production plants, Spiegel said.

articles.title: How long would it take the world to run out of clothing if production suddenly stopped?
articles.text:
How long would it take to run out of clothing if production stopped?
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Oct 2, 2026
How long would it take the world to run out of clothing if production suddenly stopped?
One expert told Marketplace that it could take up to 20 years. People would start tapping into textile waste dumps around the world and, of course, their own closets.
I've Always Wondered ...by Janet Nguyen
If clothing production stopped, it might take us decades to run through the current supply. But getting your hands on a pair of jeans is still easy at the moment.
ozgurdonmaz/Getty Images
This is just one of the stories from our “I’ve Always Wondered” series, where we tackle all of your questions about the world of business, no matter how big or small. Ever wondered if recycling is worth it? Or how store brands stack up against name brands? Check out more from the series here.
Anne Crabbe from Paso Robles, California, asks:
I've always wondered how long it would take for the world to run out of clothes if all production of clothes stopped at once. There are SO many clothes out there (at least here in North America). If the entire world had to use the current supply of all the clothes existing now, when would stores run out? TJ Maxx, Nordstrom Rack, all the thrift stores. I assume (and hope), we would run out of under garments first, then socks, maybe? A ton of assumptions have to be made to answer this, but can it even be answered?
Billions and billions of items of clothing are produced each year, but if clothing production suddenly stopped, snapping up all those garments might take less time than you might think
Depending on your assumptions, it might take up to 20 years for the world to run out of clothing, said Julia DeVoy, who studies the fast-fashion industry and serves as dean of undergraduate programs and students at the Boston College Lynch School of Education and Human Development.
And yes, undergarments and socks would be the first to go, she said.
There would also be a gold rush for materials with higher-quality fiber, like cotton and denim.
"People would want that more, whether it's getting it at a thrift store, or grabbing whatever was on the shelves, or trading with other people who had closets. And there would also be a radical shift towards mending," DeVoy said.
DeVoy estimates that discount and big-box stores in the U.S. would take one month to run out of clothing. These stores operate a just-in time model, which means they only get clothing as needed.
TJX, the parent company of T.J. Maxx and Marshalls, reported its days inventory at 70 days as of mid-2026, which means that shelves would last nine to 10 weeks with zero restocking based on normal demand, DeVoy said. TJX arrives at this figure by taking the existing inventory and dividing it by the current sales rate, DeVoy explained.
But if clothing production stopped, then demand would go up.
"What happened during the pandemic with certain products? People thought they couldn't get hand sanitizer,” DeVoy said. “Basically, what would happen is all the stock on the shelves, because of the just-in-time [model] and the lean inventory that actually sits in the stores, there would be a panic, and all of the existing stock would be wiped out from the store themselves,"
During COVID-19 stockpiling, sales of household staples spiked between 70% to 170% above normal, and spending on stock-up categories ran 70% to 80% above the daily average, DeVoy said.
So if we assume that panic buying doubled demand, which is a conservative estimate, then that would halve the amount of time it would normally take for clothing to run out, leaving discount stores about four to five weeks before clothing ran out, DeVoy said.
People would also look to thrift stores. Thrift stores are overwhelmed with donations, but they only use about 20% to 30% of the items they receive, DeVoy said. "The remaining 70% to 80% is currently exported, incinerated, or landfilled. This is not because it's all unsellable, but because the humongous volume exceeds available shelf capacity," DeVoy said.
But even if they sold their full backlog instead of incinerating it, DeVoy said they would still sell out in a matter of months.
As stores across the country ran out of clothing, people could tap into other sources that would probably become available. About 100 billion garments are produced a year, with 45 billion garments never reaching the buyer. This is referred to as "dead stock," which means they're never sold or end up incinerated, DeVoy said.
"There would be this giant hidden reserve that we would keep probably for about the first five years," DeVoy said.
If eight billion people received a modest one to two garments per year, each, that works out to eight to 16 billion garments annually. If there are 45 billion garments, that means there would be three to five years of deadstock, DeVoy said.
There are also massive textile waste dumps around the world, which would now become a vital resource of clothing, and there's a huge surplus of clothing in people's homes, DeVoy said.
The Atacama Desert in Chile receives 131,000 tons of used textiles annually, with over 70%, or 92,000 tons, going directly into landfills or in other illegal dumps, while Ghana's Kantamanto market in Accra receives about 15 million garments a week, of which over 40% becomes direct textile waste, DeVoy said.
"Comparable sites exist all over Southeast Asia, Africa, and Latin America," DeVoy said.
And people normally only wear 20% of the clothing that they own, with Americans buying 68 new clothing items a year, so they could use the remaining 80% of clothing that's sitting in their closets, DeVoy said.
She estimates that both of these sources of clothing could stretch around 15 years.

articles.title: Not everything is suffering from inflation
articles.text:
Inflation hasn't breached every sector of the economy — yet
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Oct 15, 2026
Not everything is suffering from inflation
The price of diesel, competition, and technological innovation are among the factors tamping down inflation in some sectors of this economy.
Agricultureby Caitlin Tan
Download
Dairy products have maintained low prices through this current period of inflation, because cows are still producing lots of milk.
Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images
As shocking as it may sound, there are some sectors of this economy where inflation isn't as bad as those topline numbers from the producer price index and consumer price index.
Food prices are the most notable: At least some foods are not experiencing a whole lot of inflation. David Anderson, a professor of livestock and food product marketing at Texas A&M University, said that has a lot to do with how much diesel it takes to get that food to your supermarket.
“How close is that agricultural product as it comes from the farm to the way us consumers buy it at the store?” he asked.
Other foods have a lot of supply right now. There are a lot of dairy cows pumping out milk, for example, so prices are low. Other foods have seen a drop in demand — like bacon.
“For a long time, we put bacon on everything,” Anderson said.
But these days, people mostly want to eat beef — and it’s expensive.
“[So,] we're not adding to the cost of that meal by putting bacon on there,” Anderson said.
Eggs prices have fallen, too. U-T Austin’s Carola Binder has noticed.
“I have my own 19 chickens, and we sell eggs,” said Carola Binder, an economics professor at the University of Texas at Austin.
Binder used to give her customers a deal for $3 a dozen, because store eggs were so pricey. But now they’re not — last year’s bird flu has simmered down.
“The flocks are recovering,” Binder said. “There's more supply, and so prices are falling.”
Another area with moderate inflation is tire prices. They’re up 0.7% for producers and 0.2% for consumers. Erin Keating, executive analyst at Cox Automotive, thinks that’s because of competition.
“Consumers can shop everywhere,” Keating said.
They can pick from Costco, Mavis, a local dealer, and more.
“Unless they literally pop one and can't drive the car any further, you will see them go around and shop for them more,” she said.
Appliance and TV prices have also declined.
“One can buy an extraordinary television, but it might only cost $200,” said Anirban Basu, CEO of Sage Policy Group. “It's easy to focus on everything that has become more expensive. But there are some items that have benefited from technological progress.”
Basu said that if it wasn’t for tariffs, wars, and immigration related labor shortages, a lot of stuff might have lower prices right now.
